g9-history-uh4-t1.overview: The Middle Ages in Europe ran from about 500 to 1500 AD, opening with the Dark Age and maturing into feudal society and the Byzantine Empire. This lesson explains the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the workings of feudalism, and the clash of Byzantium with the Seljuk Turks.
objectives: Describe the main features of the medieval period in Europe
Explain what the Dark Age was and why it was so called
Analyse the components of feudal society, including vassalage and the manor
Examine the main features of the Byzantine Empire
Recognise the merits and demerits of the medieval period
g9-history-uh4-t1.simple: The Middle Ages in Europe lasted from about 500 to 1500 AD and opened with the Dark Age, the years 500 to 1000 AD, when the Western Roman Empire fell and Greco-Roman civilization declined after invasions by Germanic and Asiatic peoples. Cities shrank, society became rural, and feudalism became the political and economic order. In feudalism a lord gave a fief, a piece of land, to a vassal who owed service in return. Kings, nobles, knights and the higher clergy ruled, while peasants, craftsmen and traders held no power and were exploited. The Church owned land and controlled religion, education and culture. In the east the Byzantine Empire continued at Constantinople and reached its height under Justinian, but it lost Asia Minor after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071.
g9-history-uh4-t1.detailed:
The Dark Age, 500 to 1000 AD. The Dark Age was a period of West European history from 500 AD to 1000 AD. It was called the Dark Age because civilization declined in Western Europe during this period. The Western Roman Empire was destroyed by both internal and external problems. Internally the empire suffered division and decay. Externally it was invaded in the 5th century AD by the Anglo Saxons and Franks from the Germanic tribes and by the Huns and Magyars from the Asiatic tribes.

Changes brought by the invasions. The invasions transformed Western Europe. Greco-Roman civilization declined, societies became rural and cities declined, and feudalism became the socio-economic and political order. Churches, castles and palaces were built, bishops and monks kept records, and the knights practised chivalry. At the same time there was much war among rulers and lords, and ordinary people suffered murders and blood feuds. Nevertheless, by about 1000 AD more stability was returning, and feudal society emerged from the Dark Ages.

Feudal society. As Western Europe fell apart, the number of separate powerful lords and vassals increased. From 500 to 1500 a new socio-political system called feudalism emerged. The ruling class was made up of kings, nobles, knights (soldiers) and the higher clergy. In the vassalage system a higher lord gave a fief to a lower lord, and the lower lord became the vassal of the higher one. A fief, or feud, is a piece of land, so feudalism was a system of holding land and providing service in exchange.

Manors and the exploited masses. The basic units of European feudalism were manors, or villages. The manorial lord exercised political, judicial and military power over the peasants of his manor. The mass of feudal society was made up of peasants, craftsmen and traders, who had no political and economic power. West European feudal society was exploitative. During feudalism the Church had authority over both the ruling class and the ordinary people; the Roman Catholic Church owned land and was responsible not only for religion but also for education and culture.

The Byzantine Empire. The Byzantine Empire was the East Roman Empire, which continued after the fall of the West Roman Empire. Its capital was Constantinople, modern Istanbul, and its official language became Greek. The Orthodox Church was officially separated from the Roman Catholic Church in 1054 and became the national church that supported the emperor. The economic base of the empire was agriculture, trade and crafts, and Byzantine architecture made use of domes and beautifully coloured glasses. Society was arranged in a hierarchy of the emperor, the higher clergy, the landowning nobility and the peasants who cultivated the land. The empire reached the height of its territory and power under Emperor Justinian, who ruled from 527 to 565.

Seljuk Turks, the Crusades and Manzikert. The Seljuk Turks began their military occupation of Asia Minor in 1040 AD and challenged the Byzantine Empire. The Byzantine Empire suffered a disastrous defeat at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, losing most of Asia Minor to Seljuk Turkish rulers and later to the Ottoman Turks. The crusades, the wars of Christian Europe against the Seljuk Turks to liberate the Christian holy lands, began in the 1090s, with the first of eight major Crusades starting in 1096. The crusades failed to crush Muslim power in the holy lands, but they protected Western Europe from foreign invasions in the east.

keyTerms.def: The period of West European history from 500 AD to 1000 AD, so called because civilization declined in Western Europe.
The socio-economic and political system of about 500 to 1500 in which land was held and service provided in exchange.
A piece of land given by a higher lord to a lower lord in the vassalage system; also called a feud.
The system that related a higher lord to a lower lord through the giving of a fief.
The basic unit of European feudalism, a village whose lord held political, judicial and military power over the peasants.
The code of conduct practised by medieval knights.
The East Roman Empire that continued after the fall of the West Roman Empire, with its capital at Constantinople.
The wars of Christian Europe against the Seljuk Turks to liberate the Christian holy lands, begun in the 1090s.

workedExamples.problem: A student says the Dark Age was dark because there was no light and no learning at all. Using the textbook, correct this view.
workedExamples.given: The Dark Age ran from 500 AD to 1000 AD and was so named because civilization declined in Western Europe after the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a period label expresses the judgement of historians about change, not a literal physical condition.
workedExamples.substitution: Apply the label to the evidence: rural societies, declined cities, but also churches, castles, palaces and monks who kept records.
workedExamples.calculation: Because churches, palaces and records still existed, learning did not disappear completely; what declined was Greco-Roman urban civilization.
workedExamples.answer: The name refers to the decline of civilization in Western Europe, not to an absence of light or of all learning.

workedExamples.problem: Using the vassalage system, explain how a knight could hold land from a noble.
workedExamples.given: A higher lord gave a fief to a lower lord, and the lower lord then became the vassal of the higher one.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: feudalism was a system of holding land and providing service in exchange.
workedExamples.substitution: The noble is the higher lord, the knight is the lower lord, and the land granted is the fief.
workedExamples.calculation: The knight receives the fief and in return owes service, so the relationship exchanges land for service.
workedExamples.answer: The noble grants the knight a fief and the knight becomes his vassal, owing service in return.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the Byzantine Empire with the Western Roman Empire after the fall of Rome.
workedExamples.given: The Byzantine Empire was the East Roman Empire, with capital Constantinople, official language Greek, and an Orthodox Church separated from Rome in 1054.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: comparison by identifying continuities and differences.
workedExamples.substitution: Western Europe fragmented into feudalism and lost Greco-Roman urban life, while the East kept a strong emperor, trade and Greek culture.
workedExamples.calculation: The East continued Roman imperial rule while the West broke into feudal lordships under the Roman Catholic Church.
workedExamples.answer: Byzantium preserved an organised empire and Orthodox Christianity, while Western Europe became a feudal society.

workedExamples.problem: Assess whether the Crusades achieved their aims.
workedExamples.given: Eight major Crusades began in the 1090s, the first starting in 1096, to liberate the holy lands from the Seljuk Turks.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: evaluate aims against outcomes.
workedExamples.substitution: The aim was to free the holy lands; the outcome was failure to crush Muslim power but protection of Western Europe from eastern invasion.
workedExamples.calculation: The main aim failed, yet a secondary defensive benefit was gained.
workedExamples.answer: The Crusades failed to liberate the holy lands permanently, but they helped shield Western Europe from invasion.

commonMistakes: Thinking the Dark Age meant that all learning stopped completely in Europe.
Believing feudalism gave political and economic power to peasants, craftsmen and traders.
Confusing a fief with the person who held it; a fief is the land itself.
Thinking the Byzantine Empire began in 1453 rather than continuing from the East Roman Empire.
Believing the Crusades captured and kept the holy lands permanently.
Forgetting that the Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches separated only in 1054.
Assuming the manorial lord had no judicial or military power over his peasants.
applications: Comparing feudal tribute collection with modern taxation, which funds schools and clinics in Ethiopia.
Rejecting the exploitation of the poor, as seen in the feudal manor, as unjust in any society.
Studying Byzantine domes alongside the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela as medieval religious architecture.
Reading the Battle of Manzikert and the Crusades as a case study of religious conflict and its long-term effects.
Using timelines and maps, such as Map 4.1 of the Byzantine Empire, to place events in order.
Debating whether a period such as the Dark Age deserves its negative label.
g9-history-uh4-t1.summary: The Middle Ages in Europe opened with the Dark Age, 500 to 1000 AD, when the Western Roman Empire fell and Greco-Roman civilization declined after invasions by Germanic and Asiatic peoples. From about 500 to 1500 feudalism organised society through fiefs, vassals, manors and an exploitative lord-peasant relationship, while the Roman Catholic Church held great authority. In the east the Byzantine Empire survived at Constantinople, reached its height under Justinian, and lost Asia Minor after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 during the era of the Crusades.

g9-history-uh4-t2.overview: During the Middle Ages Asia saw the rise and rapid expansion of Islam, the growth of the Ottoman Turkish Empire, and the working of China's dynastic cycle. This lesson traces these developments and their effects on world history.
objectives: Describe the main features of the medieval period in Asia
Explain the rise and expansion of Islam throughout the world
Discuss the expansion of the Ottoman Empire and its relationship with Europe
Explain the dynastic cycle and the mandate of Heaven in China
Analyse the contribution of Asian civilizations to the medieval world
g9-history-uh4-t2.simple: During the Middle Ages Asia saw three great developments. First, Islam arose in the Arabian Peninsula around 610 AD, when the Prophet Mohammed taught in Mecca. Persecuted by the Quraysh Arabs, he and his followers moved to Medina in 622 AD, a journey called the Hejira that began the Islamic calendar. After his death the Arab caliphates of the Umayyad and then Abbasid dynasties built an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia. Second, the Seljuk and then the Ottoman Turks spread Islam by conquest; the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and renamed it Istanbul. Third, in China dynasties rose and fell in a dynastic cycle: a dynasty ruled well, then became corrupt, lost the mandate of Heaven and was replaced.
g9-history-uh4-t2.detailed:
The rise of Islam. The rise of Islam in the early seventh century AD was a great event in the history of the world. Islam began in the Arabian Peninsula with the life and teaching of the Prophet Mohammed in Mecca around 610 AD. The term Islam means submission to the will of Allah (God), and those who worship Allah are called Muslims. Islam was opposed by the Quraysh Arabs, who persecuted the Prophet and his followers, so in 622 AD the Prophet and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina. This journey is called the Hejira, and it marked the beginning year of the Islamic calendar.

Arab conquests and the caliphates. The Muslim Arabs changed the political, religious and social structures of the Near East and Middle East countries. After the death of the Prophet, Muslims came under the Arab Caliphates of the Umayyad and then the Abbasid dynasties. The death of the Prophet was followed by the great Arab conquests that established a Muslim Arab empire from North Africa and Spain in the west to Central Asia in the east. The military occupation of Palestine, Asia Minor and Arabia by the Seljuk and Ottoman Turks also contributed to the expansion of Islam.

The Ottoman Empire. The Seljuk Turks began their military occupation of Palestine, Asia Minor and Arabia in 1040. By the end of the 13th century the Ottoman Turks had replaced them, taking their name from their chief Osman, or Othman. The empire was centred in what is now Turkey, and so was called the Ottoman Turkish Empire. The Ottomans seized Anatolia in 1336 and made it their capital. At its height the empire captured Adrianople in 1356 and Salonika in 1387, defeated the Serbs in 1389 and the Bulgarians in 1393, and by the 15th century had conquered the Balkan Peninsula, including Greece.

From Constantinople to Vienna and Lepanto. In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople, renamed it Istanbul and made it their capital. They conquered Syria in 1516 and Egypt in 1517. In 1529 European forces successfully defended Vienna, the capital of Austria, from a Turkish attack, and Turkish expansion in Europe ended in 1571 when European fleets defeated the Turkish navy at the Battle of Lepanto, near Greece.

Ottoman society and its hold on trade. The Ottomans formed a group of highly trained soldiers called janissaries, and they spread Islam throughout the empire. They gained wealth from trade and controlled the trade route from Europe to Asia, banning European merchants from going to the Far East. Ottoman Turkish society was divided into four social groups: the Sultan, the grand viziers (bureaucrats), the janissaries (soldiers) and occupational groups. The culture of the Ottoman Empire was that of the Islamic world.

The dynastic cycle in China. The Chinese created a great civilization that greatly impacted other countries in East Asia, particularly Korea and Japan. In politics the Chinese accepted the idea of a dynastic cycle. When a new dynasty took power it used to be strong, ruled well and had the support of the people. However, when it became corrupt and weak and lost that support, it lost the mandate of Heaven, meaning its authority and legitimacy to rule China. It was then replaced by another new dynasty, probably founded by a rebel, and the cycle was repeated. A long succession of imperial dynasties ruled China from the Qin to the Qing, which was ended by a revolution in 1911/1912.

keyTerms.def: Submission to the will of Allah (God); the religion that began in the Arabian Peninsula around 610 AD.
The journey of the Prophet Mohammed and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD, which began the Islamic calendar.

The supreme ruler of the Ottoman Empire, at the head of its four social groups.
The Turkish empire centred on what is now Turkey and named after its chief Osman, which made Constantinople (Istanbul) its capital.
The Chinese idea that a dynasty rises when it rules well and falls when it becomes corrupt, to be replaced by another dynasty.
The authority and legitimacy to rule China, believed to be lost by a corrupt and weak dynasty.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Prophet Mohammed and his followers move from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD?
workedExamples.given: Islam began in Mecca around 610 AD, where the Quraysh Arabs opposed and persecuted the Prophet and his followers.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: cause and effect - persecution produced migration.
workedExamples.substitution: The persecution in Mecca is the cause; the Hejira to Medina is the effect.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the followers faced persecution, they moved to a safer city, and the event began the Islamic calendar.
workedExamples.answer: They moved because of persecution by the Quraysh Arabs; the journey is the Hejira and marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

workedExamples.problem: Using the four social groups of the Ottoman Empire, place them in order of importance.
workedExamples.given: Ottoman society was divided into the Sultan, grand viziers (bureaucrats), janissaries (soldiers) and occupational groups.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a social hierarchy ranks groups by power and function.
workedExamples.substitution: The Sultan stood at the top, then the grand viziers, then the janissaries, then the occupational groups.
workedExamples.calculation: Ordering the four groups by authority gives the structure of Ottoman society.
workedExamples.answer: Sultan, grand viziers, janissaries, occupational groups.

workedExamples.problem: A Chinese emperor's dynasty has become corrupt and has lost the support of the people. Using the dynastic cycle, what happens next?
workedExamples.given: When a dynasty is strong and rules well it keeps the mandate of Heaven; when it is corrupt and weak it loses it.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the dynastic cycle and the mandate of Heaven.
workedExamples.substitution: A corrupt and weak dynasty has lost the mandate of Heaven.
workedExamples.calculation: Losing the mandate means losing legitimacy, so the dynasty is replaced by a new one, perhaps founded by a rebel.
workedExamples.answer: The dynasty loses the mandate of Heaven and is replaced by a new dynasty, and the cycle repeats.

workedExamples.problem: How did Ottoman control of trade between Europe and Asia help lead to European exploration?
workedExamples.given: The Ottomans controlled the trade route from Europe to Asia and banned European merchants from going to the Far East.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a trade blockade encourages the search for alternative routes.
workedExamples.substitution: Europe needed Asian goods but could not freely use the old route.
workedExamples.calculation: The need to bypass the Ottoman blockade pushed Europeans to find new sea routes.
workedExamples.answer: The Ottoman blockade pushed Europeans to seek sea routes that bypassed Ottoman territory.

commonMistakes: Thinking Islam began in Medina; it began in Mecca around 610 AD.
Confusing the Hejira with the calendar itself instead of the journey of 622 AD that started the calendar.
Believing the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1529, when that year refers to the defence of Vienna.
Thinking the Ottomans replaced the Seljuks in 1040, when the replacement came by the end of the 13th century.
Mixing up the Huguenots and the Presbyterians, which belong to the Reformation, not to Ottoman history.
Treating the mandate of Heaven as a written constitution rather than a belief about legitimacy to rule.
Forgetting that Turkish expansion in Europe ended at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571.

Studying how control of trade routes shaped relations between Europe, the Ottoman Empire and the wider world.

g9-history-uh4-t2.summary: Islam arose in the Arabian Peninsula around 610 AD, and the Hejira of 622 AD began both the Muslim community at Medina and the Islamic calendar. After the Prophet's death the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates built an empire from Spain to Central Asia, and the Seljuk and Ottoman Turks spread Islam by conquest. The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and renamed it Istanbul, conquered Syria and Egypt, and saw their European expansion end at Lepanto in 1571. In China the dynastic cycle and the mandate of Heaven explained how dynasties rose and fell from the Qin to the Qing.

g9-history-uh4-t3.overview: Early capitalism grew out of the revival of towns and long-distance trade in the later Middle Ages. This lesson explains what distinguished capitalism from earlier systems and which historical events encouraged it.
objectives: Explain the development of early capitalism
Define capital and describe how it was used differently from earlier systems
Describe the revival of towns and trade after the collapse of the Roman Empire
Identify the problems that hindered long-distance trade
Value the importance of early capitalist relations to the modern world
g9-history-uh4-t3.simple: Early capitalism developed in the later Middle Ages as towns and trade revived after the collapse of the Roman Empire. What made capitalism different from earlier systems was that accumulated capital was used to enlarge productive capacity instead of being spent on unproductive things such as pyramids and cathedrals. Old Roman cities were restored and became centres of production and exchange, where merchants bought raw materials, paid workers to manufacture goods, and sold the finished products at the best prices. The Crusades helped revive trade, and city-states became the centres of economic and political life in Italy. Long-distance trade brought big profits but suffered from transport difficulties, war and robbery, and heavy tolls. After the discoveries, overseas trade and colonial conquest made capitalism grow faster.
g9-history-uh4-t3.detailed:
What distinguished capitalism. The development that distinguished capitalism from previous systems was the use of accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity, rather than to invest in economically unproductive enterprises such as pyramids and cathedrals. In earlier systems wealth was often spent on monuments and display, but under early capitalism it was put back into production so that more goods and more profit could be produced. This characteristic was encouraged by several historical events.

The revival of towns and trade. Most ancient cities and towns in Europe had been ruined following the collapse of the Roman Empire. However, trade revived slowly and old Roman cities were restored. The towns were the centres of production and exchange. Merchants learned how to buy raw materials, have workers do the manufacturing and sell finished products at the best prices. In this way a merchant class that lived on trade and production, rather than only on land, began to grow.

The role of the Crusades. The crusades contributed to the revival of trade in the Middle Ages. Contact with the East brought new goods and new tastes to Europe, and Italian towns in particular grew rich by carrying goods between the eastern Mediterranean and European markets. City-states were the political, economic and social life centres in Renaissance Italy, and their wealth rested on this commerce.

Long-distance trade and its problems. After the discoveries, the new long-distance international trade was important, and big profits could be made. Trade, however, faced serious problems: chiefly transport difficulties, insecurity caused by war and robbery, and heavy tolls, or taxes, often charged on the transit of commodities. These costs raised the price of goods and limited the volume of trade.

From trade to capitalism. The growing profits of trade and production were accumulated as capital. When this capital was invested in workshops, ships and further trade instead of being spent on unproductive display, productive capacity grew. The new long-distance international trade after the discoveries, together with the subsequent colonial conquest, promoted the faster development of capitalism and strengthened the connection between Europe and the rest of the world.

keyTerms.def: Accumulated wealth, such as money and goods, that can be invested in production and trade.
An economic system in which accumulated capital is used to enlarge productive capacity rather than spent on unproductive enterprises.
The ability of an economy to produce more goods, which early capitalism increased by reinvesting capital.
A trader who buys raw materials, has workers manufacture goods and sells the finished products.
A centre of production and exchange, many of which were revived after the collapse of the Roman Empire.
Heavy taxes charged on the transit of commodities, which raised prices and hindered trade.
International trade over great distances, which after the discoveries brought big profits and promoted capitalism.
Independent towns, such as those in Renaissance Italy, that were political, economic and social life centres.

workedExamples.problem: A ruler spends the wealth of the kingdom on building a huge cathedral, while a merchant spends his wealth on ships and workshops. Which behaviour is capitalist, and why?
workedExamples.given: Early capitalism used accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity rather than invest in economically unproductive enterprises such as pyramids and cathedrals.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: capital is allocated either to unproductive display or to productive investment.
workedExamples.substitution: The cathedral is unproductive display, while the ships and workshops are productive investments.
workedExamples.calculation: Only the merchant puts capital back into production so that more goods and profit can be produced.
workedExamples.answer: The merchant is behaving in a capitalist way, because the capital is reinvested in production rather than spent on display.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why heavy tolls slowed the growth of long-distance trade.
workedExamples.given: Trade problems included transport difficulties, insecurity caused by war and robbery, and heavy tolls often charged on the transit of commodities.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: costs and risks reduce the volume of trade.
workedExamples.substitution: A toll is an added cost that the merchant passes on in the price of the goods.
workedExamples.calculation: Higher costs reduce demand and profit, so fewer goods are carried and trade grows more slowly.
workedExamples.answer: Heavy tolls raised prices and cut profits, so merchants traded less and long-distance trade grew slowly.

workedExamples.problem: How did the Crusades help revive trade in medieval Europe?
workedExamples.given: The crusades contributed to the revival of trade in the Middle Ages, and city-states became the political, economic and social life centres in Renaissance Italy.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: contact and exchange stimulate commerce.
workedExamples.substitution: The Crusades brought Europeans into direct contact with the eastern Mediterranean and its goods.
workedExamples.calculation: New goods and tastes created demand, and Italian towns profited by carrying goods between East and West.
workedExamples.answer: The Crusades increased contact and demand, and Italian towns grew rich carrying eastern goods to European markets.

workedExamples.problem: How did the voyages of discovery and colonial conquest promote the development of capitalism?
workedExamples.given: After the discoveries, big profits could be made from the new long-distance international trade, and the newly discovered lands became colonies of European powers.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: overseas trade and colonies supplied profit that was reinvested as capital.
workedExamples.substitution: The profits of trade and the wealth taken from colonies were accumulated in Europe.
workedExamples.calculation: Accumulated capital invested in further production and trade enlarged productive capacity and speeded up capitalism.
workedExamples.answer: Overseas trade and colonial wealth produced profits that were reinvested, so capitalism developed faster.

commonMistakes: Thinking capitalism means only the possession of money, rather than the productive use of accumulated capital.
Believing early capitalism first appeared only after the Industrial Revolution instead of in the later Middle Ages.
Assuming towns disappeared forever after the collapse of the Roman Empire.
Forgetting that heavy tolls, war, robbery and poor transport all hindered long-distance trade.
Believing the Crusades had only religious effects and no economic consequences.
Thinking merchants simply sold goods they made by hand themselves rather than organising production and exchange.
Treating city-states as purely cultural centres with no economic or political role.
applications: Comparing how Ethiopian traders and small businesses reinvest profits with the early capitalist use of capital.
Recognising that money invested in tools, farms and workshops can create more wealth than money spent only on display.
Studying the effect of transport costs and taxes on the price of goods traded in Ethiopian markets.
Discussing how trade routes and ports connect Ethiopia with the wider world economy.
Valuing productive work and saving as habits that build a stronger economy.
Using a flow chart to trace how trade profits can become capital and then production.
g9-history-uh4-t3.summary: Early capitalism developed as towns and trade revived after the collapse of the Roman Empire. It was distinguished from earlier systems by the use of accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity instead of spending it on unproductive enterprises such as pyramids and cathedrals. The Crusades helped revive trade, towns became centres of production and exchange, and long-distance trade earned big profits despite transport difficulties, war, robbery and heavy tolls. After the discoveries, overseas trade and colonial conquest promoted the faster development of capitalism.

g9-history-uh4-t4.overview: In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries European sailors opened sea routes to Asia, the Americas and around the world. This lesson explains why Europeans explored, who the explorers were, and what the discoveries changed.
objectives: Describe the age of European explorations and discoveries
Explain the factors that encouraged exploration, including the Ottoman blockade
Identify the leading explorers and the lands they reached
Analyse the economic impacts of the discoveries
Evaluate the effects of the discoveries on the wider world
g9-history-uh4-t4.simple: The age of European explorations and discoveries took place in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. It was driven partly by the need to bypass the Ottoman Turkish blockade of the old trade route from Europe to the Far East. Europeans were also encouraged by interest in long-distance trade, the compass, better maps and ships, and the growth of geographical knowledge. Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal (1394-1460) and Queen Isabella of Spain (1451-1504) sponsored voyages for economy, religion and glory. Portugal and Spain led, closely followed by Holland, Britain, France and Russia. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498, Christopher Columbus reached America in 1492, and Ferdinand Magellan's expedition sailed around the world from 1519 to 1522. The new lands became European colonies.
g9-history-uh4-t4.detailed:
What the age of exploration was. The age of European explorations and discoveries was in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The explorations were, in part, initiated by the need to bypass the Ottoman Turkish blockade of the old long-distance trade route from Europe to the Far East. Because the Ottomans controlled and charged tolls on the overland route to Asia, Europeans had a strong motive to find another way to reach the rich markets of the East.

Factors that encouraged exploration. Several factors encouraged explorations and discoveries. There was a European interest in long-distance trade and in new inventions like the compass. In addition, the development of better maps and ships and the growing interest in geographical knowledge fuelled the idea of exploration. Powerful rulers also inspired it: Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal (1394-1460) and Queen Isabella of Spain (1451-1504), who supported the voyages of explorers and sponsored them for the sake of their economy, religion and glory. Spain and Portugal were the leaders in exploration and discoveries in the 15th and 16th centuries, and they were closely followed by Holland, Britain, France and Russia.

Portuguese and Spanish voyages. The Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama discovered a new sea route to India and the Far East in 1498. Christopher Columbus was the first European explorer to reach America in 1492, while he was in the service of Spain. Unfortunately, Columbus died without knowing that he had found new lands. The land found came to be known as America, from the name of an Italian mapmaker called Amerigo Vespucci, and the newly discovered areas also became known as the New World. The Portuguese Ferdinand Magellan circumnavigated the world between 1519 and 1522 in the service of Spain.

Conquest and colonies. The newly discovered lands were later conquered and became colonies of European powers. Exploration therefore had consequences far beyond navigation: European states claimed territory, extracted wealth and governed peoples in the Americas, Asia and Africa. The voyages marked the beginning of a wider colonial era in world history.

Economic impacts. There were economic impacts of the age of exploration and discoveries. Economically, Europeans gained huge profits from local trade networks, which enhanced the globalising process. Moreover, with the subsequent colonial conquest, the voyages promoted the faster development of capitalism. The trade in new goods and the wealth of the colonies fed the growth of towns, merchants and overseas commerce in Europe.

g9-history-uh4-t5.overview: The Renaissance was an intellectual movement that began in Italy and spread across Europe, reviving the learning of ancient Greece and Rome and placing new emphasis on human ability. This lesson explains its features, its great figures and its lasting influence.
objectives: Define the Renaissance and explain the meaning of the word
Describe the three main features of Renaissance Italy
List the characteristics of Renaissance thought and art
Identify the outstanding persons and works of the Renaissance
Compare the ideals of the Renaissance with today's world thinking
g9-history-uh4-t5.simple: The Renaissance was an intellectual movement, and the word means rebirth of learning. It began in Italy in the 14th century and ended in the 17th century, spreading to England, France, Germany, Spain and Holland. Renaissance Italy was an urban society; it was an age of recovery from the disasters of the fourteenth century; and it produced a new view of human beings that emphasised individual ability. Its characteristics were the study of ancient Roman and Greek languages, literature and arts and the use of reason; freedom of thought and a questioning mind; and the use of the vernacular, or national language, instead of Latin. Great figures included Dante, Thomas More, Cervantes, Shakespeare, Leonardo da Vinci, Michael Angelo, Vesalius and Copernicus.
g9-history-uh4-t5.detailed:
What the Renaissance was. The Renaissance was an intellectual movement, and the word renaissance indicates the rebirth of learning. It began in the 14th century and ended in the 17th century. The Renaissance began in Italy and spread to the rest of Europe, mainly to England, France, Germany, Spain and Holland.

Three features of Renaissance Italy. First, Renaissance Italy was essentially an urban society. Second, the Renaissance was an age of recovery from the disasters of the fourteenth century, and this revival affected both politics and art. Third, a new view of human beings emerged, as people in the Italian Renaissance began to emphasise individual ability.

Characteristics of the Renaissance. The Renaissance had the following characteristics: the study of ancient Roman and Greek languages, literature and arts and the use of reason; the support of freedom of thought and a questioning mind; and the use of the vernacular, or the national language such as Italian and English, rather than Latin in writing.

Literature. The outstanding persons of the Renaissance produced great works of literature. The Divine Comedy was written by the Italian Dante Alighieri; Utopia by the Englishman Thomas More; Don Quixote by the Spaniard Cervantes; the Holy Bible was translated into German by Martin Luther; and various great plays were written by the Englishman William Shakespeare.

Art. In the arts, the Italian Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper and the Monalisa, while the Italian Michael Angelo painted the Creation of Adam and made statues of David, Moses and the Virgin and the dead Christ.

Science. In science, the Belgian Vesalius studied human anatomy, and the Polish Nicholas Copernicus declared that the earth revolved around the sun. Previously, it was thought that the planets revolved around the earth.

Influence on the modern world. The Renaissance had a profound influence on the development of modern society and culture. Its influence brought about a new focus on humanism and, as a result, a turning away from the dominant ideas put forth by the church. The dawning recognition of human potential and scientific inquiry shaped the course of world history and still influences contemporary societies and culture today.

workedExamples.answer: They placed human beings and human ability at the centre of art and learning, which is humanism.

g9-history-uh4-t5.summary: The Renaissance was an intellectual movement, meaning rebirth of learning, that began in Italy in the 14th century and ended in the 17th, spreading to England, France, Germany, Spain and Holland. It was an urban movement, an age of recovery, and it produced a new emphasis on individual ability. Its characteristics were the study of ancient Greece and Rome and the use of reason, freedom of thought, and writing in the vernacular. Great figures such as Dante, Thomas More, Cervantes, Shakespeare, Leonardo da Vinci, Michael Angelo, Vesalius and Copernicus advanced literature, art and science, and the movement gave the modern world its focus on humanism and scientific inquiry.

g9-history-uh4-t6.overview: The Reformation was a religious movement of the early 16th century that produced Protestantism and split Western Christianity. This lesson explains its causes, its main churches, the Catholic response and its long wars.
objectives: Define the Reformation and its place in the 16th century
Explain the social, political, religious and economic causes of the Reformation
Identify the Protestant churches and their founders
Describe the Catholic Counter-Reformation and the Society of Jesus
Compare the ideals of the Reformation with today's world thinking
g9-history-uh4-t6.simple: The Reformation was a religious movement that led to the emergence of Protestantism from the Catholic Church at the beginning of the 16th century. It began in Germany, led by Martin Luther in 1517, for social, political, religious and economic reasons. Protestant reformers supported capitalism, individualism and nation-states, and they formed many churches: Jean Calvin established a Calvinist church in Switzerland, his French followers were called Huguenots, John Knox founded Presbyterianism in Scotland in 1560, and Henry VIII and Elizabeth I separated the English church, which became the Anglican Church. The Catholic Church responded with the Counter-Reformation, including the Society of Jesus founded by Ignatius Loyola in 1534. The Reformation helped cause the Thirty Years' War, ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
g9-history-uh4-t6.detailed:
What the Reformation was. The Reformation was a religious movement that led to the emergence of Protestantism from the Catholic Church at the beginning of the 16th century. It began in Germany, led by Martin Luther in 1517. The causes were social, political, religious and economic.

Protestant ideas and churches. The Protestant reformers supported the principles of capitalism, individualism and nation-states. They established various Protestant Churches. For instance, the French protestant Jean Calvin, who lived in Switzerland, established a Calvinist protestant church in Switzerland, and the Calvinist followers in France were called Huguenots. The Scottish reformer John Knox founded his type of Calvinist Protestantism called Presbyterian in 1560. King Henry VIII and Queen Elizabeth I separated the English Protestant Church from the Roman Catholic Church in England, and the English Protestants managed to establish a national church which came to be called the Anglican Church.

The Catholic Counter-Reformation. Protestantism forced the Catholic Church into the Counter-Reformation. The Catholic Church carried out the Catholic Counter-Reformation to reform itself in response to the Protestant challenge of the time. A missionary organisation called the Society of Jesus was formed in Spain by Ignatius Loyola in 1534 to reform Catholics in America, Asia and Africa. The members of the society were called Jesuits and were active in the Americas. Anti-Catholics were attacked and even killed.

Wars and the Peace of Westphalia. The peasants' wars of Germany against Catholics were fought between 1524 and 1525. The Reformation played an essential role in the Thirty Years' War, which lasted from 1618 to 1648. The Peace of Westphalia ended the war in Germany in 1648.

Why it mattered. The Reformation permanently divided Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant branches, and it strengthened the ideas of individualism, capitalism and the nation-state. Its long and destructive wars also taught Europe the importance of settling disputes by peaceful means, an idea that is still relevant to the world today.

g9-history-uh4-t6.summary: The Reformation was a religious movement that produced Protestantism from the Catholic Church at the beginning of the 16th century, beginning in Germany under Martin Luther in 1517 for social, political, religious and economic reasons. Protestant reformers, supporting capitalism, individualism and nation-states, formed churches such as the Calvinist church in Switzerland, the Huguenot and Presbyterian movements and the Anglican Church of England. The Catholic Church replied with the Counter-Reformation and the Society of Jesus founded by Ignatius Loyola in 1534. The Reformation was central to the Thirty Years' War, which ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

g9-history-uh4-t7.overview: The Industrial Revolution replaced hand labour with machines and factories, beginning in Great Britain in the 1780s. This lesson explains the new steam power, the growth of industry and how industrialisation spread to other nations.
objectives: Define the Industrial Revolution
Explain how steam power replaced wind and water power
Describe how steam was applied to transport by river, sea and railway
Explain why Great Britain became the first industrial nation
List the contributions of the Industrial Revolution to the modern world
g9-history-uh4-t7.simple: The Industrial Revolution was the invention and use of machines in place of hard labour. Machines now did work that had been done by hand with simple tools. Europe shifted from an economy based on farming and handicrafts to one based on manufacturing by machine in factories. It began in Great Britain in the 1780s and took several decades to spread to other Western nations. The new machine power was steam, which replaced the early wind and water power. Savry and Newcomer built early steam engines, and James Watt improved them between 1782 and 1784 and applied them to all kinds of machinery and to transport by steamboat, steamship and railway. The first railway locomotive was built in 1804. By the mid-nineteenth century Britain was the world's first and richest industrial nation.
g9-history-uh4-t7.detailed:
What the Industrial Revolution was. The term Industrial Revolution means the invention and use of machines in place of hard labour. Machines now did work that had previously been done by hand with simple tools and equipment. Europe saw a shift from an economy based on farming and handicrafts to an economy based on manufacturing by machine in factories. It began in Great Britain in the 1780s and took several decades to spread to other Western nations.

Steam power. The machines of the Industrial Revolution were operated by a new form of power known as steam power, which replaced the early wind and water power. Savry built an early steam device in 1698, and Newcomer worked on steam engines around 1705 to 1711. James Watt then improved the steam engines between 1782 and 1784 and adopted them for operating all kinds of machinery, including the machines in factories.

Steam and transport. Steam power was then applied to transport. The first steamboat appeared on the rivers, followed by steamships at sea. Finally, steam power was used for land transport in the form of railways, and the first railway locomotive was built in 1804.

Britain, the first industrial nation. By the mid-nineteenth century, Great Britain had become the world's first and richest industrial nation. Its cotton industry alone in 1850 was equal in size to the industries of all other European countries combined. Britain began first because it had abundant natural resources, a large labour force to work in the new factories, and the readiness to invest in the new industrial machines.

Spread beyond Britain. The Industrial Revolution also occurred in the United States in 1800. Britain was the leading industrial nation in the early and mid-nineteenth century, but countries like the United States eventually surpassed Britain in industrial production. The Industrial Revolution spread to the rest of Europe at different times and speeds, and the first to be industrialised in continental Europe were Belgium, France and Germany.

workedExamples.problem: Using the textbook definition, explain why the change from hand tools to machines is called a revolution.
workedExamples.given: The term Industrial Revolution means the invention and use of machines in place of hard labour, and Europe shifted from an economy based on farming and handicrafts to one based on manufacturing by machine in factories.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a revolution is a deep and lasting change in the way society works.
workedExamples.substitution: The change affected not one craft but the whole economy, moving production into factories.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the whole basis of production and work changed, the word revolution is justified.
workedExamples.answer: It is called a revolution because machines replaced human labour and the whole economy shifted to factory manufacturing.

workedExamples.problem: Order these developments in the use of steam: railways, steamships at sea, steamboats on rivers.
workedExamples.given: Steam power was applied first to the first steamboat on the rivers, then to steamships at sea, and finally to land transport in the form of railways.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skills method: order events by the sequence given in the source.
workedExamples.substitution: River transport comes first, then sea, then land railway.
workedExamples.calculation: Following the source sequence gives the order of application.
workedExamples.answer: Steamboats on rivers, then steamships at sea, then railways on land.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why Great Britain became the starting place of the Industrial Revolution.
workedExamples.given: Britain had abundant natural resources, a large labour force to work in the new factories, and the readiness to invest in the new industrial machines.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: an industrial take-off needs resources, labour and capital together.
workedExamples.substitution: Natural resources supply materials, the labour force supplies workers, and investment supplies the machines.
workedExamples.calculation: Because Britain had all three conditions at once, it industrialised first.
workedExamples.answer: Britain had abundant natural resources, a large labour force and the willingness to invest, so it industrialised first.

workedExamples.problem: A statement says Britain's cotton industry in 1850 was smaller than the cotton industries of other European countries. Is this consistent with the textbook?
workedExamples.given: By the mid-nineteenth century Britain was the world's first and richest industrial nation, and its cotton industry alone in 1850 was equal in size to the industries of all other European countries combined.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skills method: test a statement against the evidence.
workedExamples.substitution: The source says the cotton industry was equal to all other European industries combined, not smaller.
workedExamples.calculation: The statement contradicts the evidence, so it is false.
workedExamples.answer: No. Britain's cotton industry alone was equal to the industries of all other European countries combined.

commonMistakes: Believing the Industrial Revolution began in France or the United States instead of Great Britain.
Placing its beginning in the 19th century rather than the 1780s.
Thinking wind and water power were the new power of the Industrial Revolution; steam replaced them.
Saying James Watt invented the steam engine from nothing, when he improved engines built earlier by Savry and Newcomer.
Forgetting that the first railway locomotive was built in 1804.
Thinking the United States was the first industrial nation, when Britain led and the United States later surpassed it.
Assuming the revolution spread everywhere at the same time and speed.
applications: Comparing handicraft production at home with factory production by machine.

g9-history-uh4-t7.summary: The Industrial Revolution was the invention and use of machines in place of hard labour, shifting Europe from farming and handicrafts to manufacturing by machine in factories. It began in Great Britain in the 1780s, using steam power that replaced wind and water, with early engines built by Savry and Newcomer and improved by James Watt between 1782 and 1784. Steam was applied to river boats, sea ships and railways, the first locomotive appearing in 1804. By the mid-nineteenth century Britain was the world's first and richest industrial nation, and the revolution later spread to the United States and to Belgium, France and Germany.
